doc.title: Byron Stripling interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 25, 2020 [interview 2 of 2]

title: Cancelling Columbus Jazz Orchestra concerts and planning the season
summary: He recounts cancelling the March concerts, paying musicians via PPP, the Pittsburgh Symphony pops debut on hold, and virtual plans.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Getting paid: wages, scale and the pay envelope

blocks.x: I appreciate your eloquent opinions. Just to wrap up, were you in the position, when all the cancellations of gigs started coming in, usually you were told, okay the gig is off, the thing is cancelled. Did you have to cancel anything yourself, out of feeling for your own protection or the thinking of your sidemen or whatever else?

Well yeah I had a number of scenarios in that, so I conduct the Columbus Jazz Orchestra and the week that the State of Ohio, the governor did a great thing and the day before our first concert he said no venues of a thousand or more can have people there. Our concerts run four nights: Thursday, Friday, Saturday and Sunday. I had two guest artists in and my full band had already done four rehearsals with those guest artists to present the concert. On Thursday, the day we were supposed to start, the governor said, actually venues, only 500 was the max you could have in your venue. That cut us out. We were rehearsing when we got that, we were onstage at our theater. We had dinner for everybody between sound check and shows. And during dinner I just talked to everybody and the one thing I did say is I said when we come back from this things will never be the same. So we cancelled all our performances — real quick, it goes to your question — we said okay well how about, we got everybody agree to do a live broadcast on FaceBook on Saturday and we found a venue that seated only 50 people, which was allowable back then at the very beginning, or in the middle of March. We go there, one of my musicians said, “Hey you know I just came back from Paris, right?” I said, “Yeah.” He said, “The singer I was

with has a horrible fever right now. I just wanted to let you know that.” And that’s when they were just starting to talk about what you need to watch out for and that was one of the things. He said, “I feel fine but I could be one of those asymptomatic guys.” And you know I just weighed that, and it was like we can’t do this. We can’t put those people on stage. Even if it’s 50, I’ve got musicians that may have been working with this guy, I don’t want to make that further, and there’s the audience. You care about the safety of everybody. So we cancelled the whole season, or the whole concert series. We were able to pay everybody for that, and we did our due diligence on that. Then within a week or so of that we applied for the Paycheck Protection Program and we were able to get that. We had an April concert which we couldn’t do, but because of that we were able to pay everybody for that, for the April concert. So I think people need to understand that as a musician every gig counts. You know this is not like sitting on, it’s what they call now the “gig economy.” It’s like you’re looking for the next gig. It’s like my first statement to you where I said I pick up the phone, “I can do it.” You know, and that’s where most of the guys in my band that I lead, the Columbus Jazz Orchestra, “Hey are we going to get an April payment” you know. And it’s so great that we could do that. But now I’ve cancelled a summer series. We played four concerts and with a rehearsal for each one of those for the guys, and I had to tell everybody that’s gone too. Now the decision I made, I apologize for keep interrupting, the decision I’ve made is we’re supposed to start in October with our new season — and I think we’re going to start in December. But what CNN told me yesterday, along with Fauci and Sanjay Gupta was we’re getting worse, we’re not getting better. So are people comfortable social distancing in December? That’s why I’ve made that either livestream or television broadcast, but I still am going to have to social distance my musicians when they play, and it goes on. I also am the principal pops conductor with the Pittsburgh Symphony. And so in that role I was supposed to do my debut concert with them in October and they’ve told me that everything is on hold. But Pittsburgh liked what I’ve done with my organization — it’s we’re not going to just shut down. There are organizations like the National Symphony who I’ve worked with a lot, and other orchestras that said we’re just done until — just cut it off.
Yeah. It would be a double whammy if you scheduled something even way down the line and then had to cancel it again.

Yes. And that’s why my backup is that we’re able to do things virtually with the band. I think that — see because nonprofits work off of season ticket sales. That’s your base of your foundation and money, in addition to donations and stuff. By the way, people are amazingly generous. I mean we’ve had people write checks to us for tens of thousands of dollars. That’s when my dad and my mom always said it pays to be nice to people. You know what I’m saying?
